related_questions.question: What is the 4% rule for retirement taxes?
related_questions.snippet: The 4% rule is a guideline for retirees to withdraw 4% of their retirement savings in the first year, adjusting the amount for inflation in subsequent years. This approach aims to provide a steady income stream while preserving the longevity of the retirement fund.

text_blocks.snippet: A retirement calculator uses estimated tax rates to project your tax liability in retirement, helping you understand how taxes will affect your retirement income. These calculators typically require you to input your expected income sources (like Social Security, pensions, and withdrawals from retirement accounts) and then estimate the applicable tax rates.
How Tax Rates Affect Retirement Planning

list.title: Income Tax Brackets:
list.snippet: Retirement income, such as withdrawals from 401(k)s, traditional IRAs, and pensions, is generally taxed as ordinary income. This means your withdrawals will be subject to the federal income tax brackets, which can range from 10% to 37%.

list.title: State Income Taxes:
list.snippet: Many states also have their own income taxes, and these will also apply to your retirement income. Some states, like California, tax retirement income at rates between 1% and 13.3%.

list.title: Social Security Taxes:
list.snippet: Up to 85% of your Social Security benefits may be taxable depending on your combined income.

list.title: Investment Income:
list.snippet: Income from investments (like dividends and capital gains) may also be subject to taxes, and your retirement calculator should account for those.

list.title: Tax-Deferred vs. Taxable Accounts:
list.snippet: If you have retirement savings in tax-deferred accounts (like 401(k)s and traditional IRAs), you'll pay taxes on withdrawals in retirement. However, if you have savings in Roth accounts, those withdrawals will generally be tax-free.

text_blocks.snippet: What to Expect from a Retirement Calculator:

list.title: Tax Rate Input:
list.snippet: Retirement calculators will often ask you to input your expected tax rate or tax bracket. You can use the IRS tax brackets to estimate your federal tax rate and factor in your state's income tax rate.

list.title: Taxable Income Projection:
list.snippet: The calculator will estimate your taxable income in retirement based on your inputs (e.g., retirement savings, Social Security benefits, pension income).

list.title: Tax Liability Calculation:
list.snippet: Using the projected taxable income and the estimated tax rates, the calculator will estimate your tax liability in retirement.

list.title: Retirement Income Analysis:
list.snippet: The calculator will then analyze how your estimated tax liability affects your overall retirement income, helping you understand if you'll have enough money to cover your expenses.

text_blocks.snippet: Let's say you expect to have $60,000 in annual income in retirement, including $30,000 from Social Security and $30,000 from withdrawals from a traditional 401(k). You also live in a state that taxes retirement income at 5%. A retirement calculator would:

list.snippet: Estimate your federal income tax bracket based on your total income and filing status.
Calculate your federal income tax on the $30,000 from your 401(k).
Determine if any portion of your Social Security is taxable based on your income and the Social Security tax rules.
Estimate your state income tax on your total income.
Sum up the federal and state taxes to get your total tax liability.
Subtract the total tax liability from your $60,000 income to estimate your net retirement income after taxes.
